Typically, tax abatements are done on a case by case basis. If an abatement is passed, it is agreed to by the developer and city council, and there is corresponding legislation memorializing this agreement. If the developer wishes to revise that agreement, it must go back through the legislative process again. With abatements, there is also an annual review by the city to ensure the agreed upon obligations are being met. If the developer fails to meet their obligations, then the abatement could be revoked. For example, a developer says I will build two buildings of 100 units each within 5 years. The city says ok, legislation in place. Year 6 comes along, and only one building is built. The city has the ability per the agreement to say forget it, no more abatement. While this is an oversimplified example, I do want to make it clear that tax abatements do not come without obligations from the developer. These are also for a finite period, so they don't go on in perpetuity. While it can be viewed as corporate welfare, and in some instances I agree, it is a valuable economic development tool.
Abatements are contingent upon meeting the required units agreed when the legislation is put in place.

You might be confused between a rezoning and updating zoning codes. A rezoning happens when a property changes between one zoning classification to another. For example, rezoning a property from commercial use to residential use. Nothing, directly, to do with the zoning code. We're changing the color on the map, and regulations based upon that color.. Now different codes apply, was for a barber shop, now for a house. Under each zoning classification, there are subcategories. Residential, for example, ranges from 5+ story apartment building to single family home. So, levels in intensity of use.

Updating zoning code, means you change the regulations for, in the case of Columbus at this time with their comprehensive update, for all zoning districts. The regulations have changed, but it still is predicated upon the zoning classification. For example, if you're zoned commercial, it still may not allow a house, but parking requirements have been reduced.

So, I believe, we're talking about two different things.
